stories.topic: Algorithmic Discovery of Shoegaze and an Old Love Rediscovered
stories.summary: Amit recounts how Spotify, off the back of his Yo La Tengo listening, served him a 'Shoegaze' playlist he'd never heard the word for. A song from a band called Galaxie 500 grabbed him, which triggered a flashback to Luna, a band he had loved in early-to-mid-90s India where alternative rock was almost impossible to procure. Galaxie 500 turned out to be Luna frontman Dean Wareham's earlier band — a connection he could never have made before streaming. He then explains shoegaze as a guitar-pedal-heavy genre whose performers stood still on stage looking down at their effects boards, hence 'shoe gaze.'
stories.insight: The algorithmic randomizer, when used as a discovery layer rather than a comfort feed, can reverse-engineer your own past. Letting playlists run, rather than curating tightly, is a low-cost way to break out of a comfort zone that ages you.

stories.topic: What Are the Two Most Recent Songs You Know?
stories.summary: A friend of Ajay's asked him to name the two most recent songs he knew and loved. His instinctive answer was 'November Rain' from 1992. After thinking carefully he could only name two: Harry Styles' 'Sign of the Times' (2017) and Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper's 'Shallow' (2018) — and even then, he had to reach for them.
stories.insight: The exercise is a quick personal audit of how much our musical lives have ossified at a particular age. It also gently rebukes the reflex to dismiss new artists — Harry Styles, on a closer listen, turns out to be 'bloody good.'

stories.topic: The Sex Workers Talking Back to Kiran Bedi
stories.summary: Amit recalls a TV show, hosted by Barkha Dutt with Kiran Bedi as a panellist, where Bedi was being moralistic about banning prostitution. Actual sex workers in the audience pushed back — they had entered the work willingly, it was the best option open to them, and they refused to be patronised. Amit uses the moment to argue that elite morality, when imposed by law, pushes the trade into the hands of the underworld, where genuine trafficking and abuse flourish.
stories.insight: Listen to the people whose lives a policy actually touches before legislating their morals. The very arguments rich panellists use to 'protect' the vulnerable end up handing those vulnerable people to criminals.

stories.summary: Back when Section 377 was still in force, Mumbai cops ran a sting on gay men. They would place ads on online bulletin boards seeking gay company, lure the respondent to a railway station — often Matunga — flash a badge, and threaten to tell the victim's wife, father, or family. They would then walk the victim to an ATM and empty his account. Amit wrote a column on it called 'The Matunga Racket' years before 377 was struck down.
stories.insight: Laws against victimless 'crimes' don't suppress behaviour — they create rents for the state's own foot-soldiers to extract. The cost is paid in extortion, terror, and ruined lives, all enabled by a sentence in a colonial-era statute.

stories.topic: The Sweatshop Ban That Sent Children to Prostitution
stories.summary: Amit cites two field studies. Oxfam in Bangladesh: roughly 30,000 children were laid off from alleged sweatshops after Western activists complained, and many girls ended up in prostitution and many boys in criminality. UNICEF in Nepal: 5,000 to 7,000 children were laid off from a carpet-manufacturing scandal, and the girls 'practically uniformly went into prostitution.' Both follow-ups went unreported by the journalists who launched the original campaigns.
stories.insight: The unseen costs of a feel-good ban are often catastrophically worse than the seen problem. The moral test of an activist isn't the campaign — it's the willingness to look at what happened to the people the campaign claimed to save.

stories.summary: At a recent party, Amit met a successful Hyderabad professional sipping a single malt who declared that he found 'the word degrowth very attractive — we should do degrowth, we've had enough growth.' Amit told him plainly that everything he was saying was deeply immoral, because growth — every 1% of which (per Nitin Pai's calculation) lifts roughly two million Indians out of poverty — was the only thing that gave the poor a chance.
stories.insight: 'Degrowth' from a single-malt glass is the purest form of luxury belief: aesthetic for the speaker, lethal for the listener. The willingness to confront a friend at a party with the moral cost of his fashionable opinion is part of the social labour of taking poverty seriously.

stories.topic: Ambedkar Argued Against Putting 'Socialist' in the Constitution
stories.summary: When the Constituent Assembly debated whether the words 'secular' and 'socialist' should appear in the Preamble, Ambedkar argued no on both. On 'secular' his point was that if the value is inscribed into every article, naming it in the Preamble is mere signalling. On 'socialist' his point was deeper: what economic system a country should have is a question for politics and the political process, not for the constitution to fix in stone. Ambedkar himself favoured a socialistic form at the time, but by the 1950s he had updated his view — Chandra Bhan Prasad's two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, and Amit suspects Ambedkar would have approved. The words were inserted by Indira Gandhi later.
stories.insight: A founder's living, updating view is too often replaced by his frozen totem. The Indira preamble is what young protesters now hold up — useful for 'secular,' but smuggling 'socialist' along for the ride. Both the freezing of a thinker and the freezing of a country's economic theology are species of the same intellectual mistake.

stories.topic: The Strongman Always Comes for the Rich Eventually
stories.summary: Ajay traces a recurring pattern. In Saudi Arabia, MBS led a shakedown of hundreds of rich people, grabbing wealth. In China, Xi Jinping mounted an attack on the rich, partly destroying and partly expropriating them. In Russia, Putin attacked the oligarchs. In each case, every individual billionaire had at some point thought, 'No, no, I am the insider — I'll get special favours.' For a while it worked. In steady state it did not.
stories.insight: Allying with the populist strongman is a chronic intellectual error of business communities that have economised on the social sciences and humanities. The only sustainable recipe for a firm's long-term value is rule of law and liberal democracy — even if expediency keeps whispering otherwise.

recommendations.item: Nowhere Near
recommendations.creator: Yo La Tengo
recommendations.context: A song Amit has been listening to a lot lately.
recommendations.reason: He calls it one of the great love songs.

recommendations.item: On Fire
recommendations.creator: Galaxie 500
recommendations.context: The early album by Dean Wareham's pre-Luna band, surfaced for Amit by a Spotify shoegaze playlist.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a brilliant album and says you've got to listen to it. It also closes a loop he couldn't have closed in 1990s India when alternative-rock back-catalogues were unfindable.

recommendations.item: Lunapark
recommendations.creator: Luna
recommendations.context: A Luna album from the early-to-mid 1990s that Amit loved as a teenager.
recommendations.reason: Recommended as the natural next step after On Fire — Dean Wareham's later band, in the same lineage.

recommendations.item: Sign of the Times
recommendations.creator: Harry Styles
recommendations.context: One of only two post-2000 songs Ajay knows and loves.
recommendations.reason: An invitation not to dismiss new artists out of hand — Harry Styles, listened to with attention, is 'bloody good.'

recommendations.item: Shallow
recommendations.creator: Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper
recommendations.context: The other post-2000 song Ajay knows and loves; from the film A Star Is Born.
recommendations.reason: Cited as further evidence that the modern era is producing worthy songs even if they don't reach an audience whose taste froze in the 1990s.

recommendations.item: Troubled: A Memoir of Foster Care, Family, and Social Class
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: Henderson's memoir of growing up in foster homes, recently spotlighted by Tyler Cowen on Marginal Revolution.
recommendations.reason: Highly recommended by Amit. Henderson is the originator of the 'luxury beliefs' framing that this entire episode is built around.

recommendations.item: Luxury Beliefs are Status Symbols
recommendations.creator: Rob Henderson
recommendations.context: The Henderson essay where the term 'luxury beliefs' is defined and developed.
recommendations.reason: The seminal short piece that gives the show its title — read it for the original framing in Henderson's own words.

recommendations.item: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42, Everything Is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on populism and the misunderstanding of words like 'populism' and 'nationalism.'
recommendations.reason: Set up the same diagnostic move used here: words people misuse because they assume the meaning matches the dictionary cognate. Helpful background to the discussion of 'socialism.'

recommendations.item: The Citizenship Battles (Episode 152, The Seen and the Unseen, with Srinath Raghavan)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive on the CAA protests.
recommendations.reason: Background reading for the episode's reflections on the protests — and the despair-tinged hope of seeing young people hold up the Indira preamble rather than Ambedkar's.

recommendations.item: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the Dalit thinker Chandra Bhan Prasad.
recommendations.reason: Source of the line that Prasad's two heroes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith — used to argue that Ambedkar's late-1950s view of capitalism was very different from his earlier socialism.

recommendations.item: Enlightenment Now
recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: Pinker's data-driven survey of human progress.
recommendations.reason: Source of the Boris and Igor parable about killing the goat — the cleanest illustration that 'fixing inequality' can mean making everyone equally poor.

recommendations.item: India's Problem Is Poverty, Not Inequality
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column distinguishing poverty from inequality.
recommendations.reason: The full version of the argument made on the show: a positive-sum world means liberalisation lifts hundreds of millions out of poverty even as inequality rises, and the two problems require opposite policy responses.

recommendations.item: On Inequality
recommendations.creator: Harry Frankfurt
recommendations.context: A slim philosophical booklet by the philosopher Harry Frankfurt.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'doctrine of sufficiency': don't level for equality, define what is enough to live on and try to get everyone above that line. A philosopher's version of the policy intuition Amit and Ajay defend.

recommendations.item: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2008 column.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of the show's argument that prohibiting prostitution, betting, and alcohol hands the trade to the underworld and worsens every problem the law claims to solve.

recommendations.item: Poker and Life (Episode 38, Everything Is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on poker.
recommendations.reason: Develops the show's stance that there is nothing immoral per se about gambling, and that legal regulated betting is preferable to underworld-run betting.

recommendations.item: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
recommendations.creator: Bruce Yandle
recommendations.context: Yandle's classic essay on regulatory coalitions.
recommendations.reason: The frame that explains why moralistic prohibitionists ('Baptists') and underworld profiteers ('bootleggers') always end up on the same side: each needs the ban to keep working. The reason Amit attacked the politics of the film Raees.

recommendations.item: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's review of the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees.
recommendations.reason: Cited as a real-world misreading: in the film, the bootlegger treats the prohibitionist politician as an enemy, but in reality they are funders and beneficiaries of each other — the Yandle dynamic in action.

recommendations.item: The Matunga Racket
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2007 column on a Mumbai police extortion racket targeting gay men under Section 377.
recommendations.reason: The case study, in real lives, of what happens when a victimless 'crime' is illegal — the policing apparatus turns into an extortion racket against the people the law was supposed to protect from sin.

recommendations.item: Why Children Labour
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2007 column on child labour, with citations to follow-up studies.
recommendations.reason: The longer version of the Bangladesh and Nepal stories — what happened to the children who were laid off when Western activists succeeded.

recommendations.item: The Economics of Child Labor
recommendations.creator: Kaushik Basu and Pham Hoang Van
recommendations.context: Basu and Van's academic paper on child-labour economics.
recommendations.reason: One of the studies that estimates the household-income threshold above which families stop sending children to work. Evidence that the long-run answer to child labour is growth, not bans.

recommendations.item: Observations on International Labor Standards and Trade
recommendations.creator: Alan B. Krueger
recommendations.context: Krueger's paper on international labour standards and trade.
recommendations.reason: A second academic source on the same threshold-of-prosperity argument — that prohibition divorced from material conditions does damage.

recommendations.item: Child Labor in the Global Economy
recommendations.creator: Eric V. Edmonds and Nina Pavcnik
recommendations.context: Edmonds and Pavcnik's paper on child labour in the global economy.
recommendations.reason: A third complementary study cited by Amit, reinforcing the empirical case that growth — not bans — is what reduces child labour.

recommendations.item: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on price controls.
recommendations.reason: The full version of the argument that price controls (on stents, on Uber, on cars in the thought experiment) hurt precisely the people they claim to protect by removing the price signal that ration scarce goods to those who need them most.

recommendations.item: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Sowell's book diagnosing the moral self-image of the policy elite.
recommendations.reason: Source of the long quote Amit reads about the anointed and the benighted: those who disagree with the prevailing vision are seen not as in error but in sin. The intellectual history of luxury beliefs.

recommendations.item: Defending the Undefendable
recommendations.creator: Walter Block
recommendations.context: Walter Block's controversial book defending professions and practices that polite society dismisses out of hand.
recommendations.reason: Amit's reading recommendation of the day. He chose it because anyone listening to this episode could fairly call him a defender of sweatshops, prostitution, and gambling — and Block's book is the canonical exercise in defending the indefensible. You don't have to agree; you have to keep talking.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Standing reference linked from the show notes — the long-form treatment of many of the policy arguments in the episode.

recommendations.item: The India Uncut Newsletter
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's newsletter at indiauncut.substack.com, recently revived to a 'furiously active' cadence.
recommendations.reason: Plugged in the description as a place to follow Amit's writing on these themes between episodes.

recommendations.item: The Art of Clear Writing
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's online writing course.
recommendations.reason: Standing recommendation linked from the show notes for listeners who want to learn to write well.

core_ideas.explanation: Rob Henderson's term, foundational for the episode. Luxury beliefs are 'ideas and opinions that confer status on the upper class while often inflicting costs on the lower classes.' The elites who profess them are insulated by their wealth — air-conditioned rooms, MacBooks, the headphones argument with themselves about which brand of noise-cancelling is funkiest — while the policies that follow from those beliefs (socialism, anti-capitalism, prohibition, price controls) wreck the lives of the poor. Amit's frame: in India, where solving poverty is a moral imperative, this is not a debating-society game.
core_ideas.quote: Luxury beliefs are ideas and opinions that confer status on the upper class while often inflicting costs on the lower classes.

core_ideas.concept: Socialism Is Coercion, Not 'Care for Society'
core_ideas.explanation: The dictionary definition of socialism is public ownership of the means of production and a heavy state hand on the rest, with individual liberty subordinate. Used as a vague vibe — 'I care about society' — the word smuggles in coercion as if it were kindness. India's socialist period kept hundreds of millions of people in poverty for decades longer than necessary, and the word still sits in the Preamble (Indira's, not Ambedkar's). Amit's two anchor concepts: consent and coercion. Socialism is the side of coercion; the 20th century was the 'history of the failure of socialism, the failure of coercion.'
core_ideas.quote: In their heart, the words I really care about and think about are consent and coercion. And socialism is equal to coercion.

core_ideas.concept: Inequality Is Not Poverty (the USA-vs-Bangladesh Test)
core_ideas.explanation: A thought experiment: would you rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh? Everyone picks the USA. The USA has more inequality; Bangladesh has more poverty. Therefore poverty, not inequality, is the variable that matters. In a positive-sum economy, growth raises everyone unequally — the poor get richer, the rich get richer faster. Liberalisation in 1991 lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty as inequality rose. Treating inequality as the priority is the goat-killing solution from Pinker's parable: equality achieved by killing what's good. Treating poverty as the priority requires growth.
core_ideas.quote: In which of these two countries would you rather be poor — the USA or Bangladesh? Everybody will say, I would rather be poor in the USA.

core_ideas.explanation: Harry Frankfurt's philosophical reframing: define what is enough for a person to live on, then try to get everyone above that line. It is not equality that matters morally but sufficiency. The doctrine has the same practical effect as a serious anti-poverty policy without making the goat-killing mistake of equating fairness with sameness. Amit uses it to translate a libertarian-economist intuition into a moral-philosophical claim.

core_ideas.concept: The Power of Compounding (200 bps Is Not a Small Number)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's arithmetic. A 'redistributionist, elite-unfriendly' Indian policy environment plausibly delivers 2% per-capita GDP growth. A pro-growth, liberty-friendly environment plausibly delivers 4%. Sounds like a small gap. But by the rule of 70, 2% doubles incomes in 35 years and quadruples in 70; 4% doubles in roughly 16 and quadruples in 32. So a granddaughter alive today is the difference between a country with one extra doubling in her lifetime, and a country with two. Compounding turns 'a little chasing of inequality' into a missing generation of prosperity.

core_ideas.concept: Victimless Crimes and the Underworld Inversion
core_ideas.explanation: When you ban a victimless act between consenting adults — prostitution, betting, alcohol, homosexuality before 377 was struck down — the activity does not stop. It migrates into the underworld, where the rule of law cannot reach it. The cops are paid off; the victims of trafficking, match-fixing, bad liquor, and extortion have nowhere to complain. The Netherlands legalised prostitution and brothels became regulated workplaces with worker rights, taxes, and low rates of violence. England taxes the casino, not the gambler. The right's moral crusade against vice consistently produces a worse version of the very vice it set out to stop.
core_ideas.quote: The point is, when the underworld is doing it, a lot of shady stuff happens, especially trafficking and coercion.

core_ideas.explanation: Bruce Yandle's regulatory-economics observation: the activist who calls for the ban (the 'Baptist') and the underworld profiteer who runs the black market (the 'bootlegger') have aligned interests. Both need the prohibition. The Baptist supplies the moral cover; the bootlegger pockets the rents. The film Raees gets it backwards by casting the bootlegger and the prohibitionist politician as enemies. In reality, they fund each other.
core_ideas.quote: The person who calls for the ban will be working towards the same purpose as a bootlegger.

core_ideas.concept: Pro-Business vs. Pro-Market Are Opposite Things
core_ideas.explanation: A core distinction Amit insists on. A business will always try to ally with the government and use state power to keep competition out — that is cronyism. True capitalism is free markets, where the state's job is rule of law and otherwise minimal interference, so the only way to get rich is to make millions of people better off (the 'double thank you' moment). The fashionable hatred of 'capitalism' from MacBook-and-AirPods elites usually conflates the two: they criticise cronyism, and they get crony bans, price controls, and licence raj as a response.
core_ideas.quote: Pro-business and pro-market can mean opposite things.

core_ideas.concept: Sweatshops and the Ethics of Respecting Agency
core_ideas.explanation: A worker chooses the sweatshop because it is the best option open to them. Banning the sweatshop does not improve the choice — it removes the best option, leaving worse ones. The Bangladesh and Nepal child-labour cases (30,000 and 5–7,000 children laid off respectively, with girls 'practically uniformly' ending up in prostitution) are the case in point. The right way to fight child labour is the long road of growth — every reputable study identifies a household-income threshold above which families stop sending children to work. The wrong way is the blunt-tool ban that lets the activist feel virtuous while the children's lives are destroyed.

core_ideas.concept: Price Controls as a Severed Information System
core_ideas.explanation: Prices are signals — they encode the world's scarcities and constraints, and they create incentives to produce more of what is needed. A price control severs that signal. The thought experiment: cap car prices at 10,000 rupees and the car industry vanishes; black markets emerge at the actual scarcity-price. The real-world example: a price control on stents created scarcity, and people died. Uber surge pricing, when the algorithm is honest, is a feature: it gets a car to the patient or the late traveller. Banning surge means first-come-first-served, which is rationing by luck, not by need.
core_ideas.quote: The price is a signal of all the scarcities in the world, all the constraints of the world, and it carries an incentive to people to produce more of them.

core_ideas.concept: Why People Hold Luxury Beliefs (the Stack of Hypotheses)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's enumerated answers to the 'why' question. (1) Pure cost-benefit: I've already got mine, costless to espouse a belief that hurts others. (2) Old-style philanthropy as protection insurance: pious phrases buy safety from the populist mob. (3) Club fashion: a costless verbal entry-ticket to elite community, unlike a Louis Vuitton bag. (4) Preference falsification (Timur Kuran): people say what they think will help them. The equilibrium requires intellectual soft-headedness — a wide doctor-engineer base with low knowledge of social science and humanities, into which the beliefs can be sprinkled. Amit adds: we lie to ourselves before we lie to others, the social-media tribe rewards purity escalation, and Sowell's 'anointed-vs-benighted' frame has been with us at least 200 years.

core_ideas.concept: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy (The Anointed)
core_ideas.explanation: Sowell's diagnosis, read out at length on the show. The prevailing vision offers its believers a 'special state of grace': those who hold it are not merely factually correct but morally on a higher plane, and those who disagree are not merely in error but in sin. The benighted are to be made aware, their consciousness raised, and if they refuse to be raised, their mean-spiritedness must be exposed. Verbal fashions change but the structure has not changed in 200 years. The connection to luxury beliefs: the policies are bad in their consequences but excellent at producing the in-group's special state of grace, which is the actual product on offer.
core_ideas.quote: Those who accept this vision are deemed to be not merely factually correct but morally on a higher plane. Those who disagree are seen as being not merely in error, but in sin.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's mechanism. Online, the easiest way to belong is to join an ideological tribe. To rise within the tribe, you uncritically accept its dogmas, then attack outsiders, then attack insiders for insufficient purity. Once you've expressed a position publicly and the tribe has rewarded you, ego makes it costly to update. The teenager Amit, with a head full of Marx and Engels, would have been petrified in his seventeen-year-old views by screenshots. The cancellation that hurts most comes from your own side, and the dynamic produces extremism by ratchet — never by argument.

core_ideas.concept: The Strongman's Protection Is a Trap (For the Rich)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's geopolitical refrain. Saudi Arabia under MBS, China under Xi, Russia under Putin — in each case a populist leader who initially looked like a friend of the rich eventually turned the knife on them. Each individual billionaire thought, 'I am the insider.' For a while it worked. In steady state it never does. The only stable equilibrium for a firm trying to compound value over decades is rule of law and liberal democracy — the boring answer that elites who have economised on humanities are forever tempted to dismiss as 'idealistic.'

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit and Ajay open by noticing they are again colour-coordinated in shades of blue: 'we both love the blues. That could be one reason.'

Ajay, after Amit reels off a chunk of music aesthetics: 'Sergei, I'm talking about art, I'm talking about music, I'm talking about the soul' — needling Amit for trying to do probability theory in the middle of a conversation about feelings.
Amit on the duet potential: 'You and I should perform Shallow sometime. I'll do the high part.'

Ajay on the rule-of-70 timeline of growth: '32 years out is an entirely feasible and a practical dimension to her life.' Amit's deadpan response: 'Thirty-two years later she'll be younger than you are.'
Amit on the etymology of 'prostitute': 'I shouldn't have even corrected the word — there's nothing wrong with the word prostitute. You and I are prostitutes — we're selling our services for money.'

Amit running a thought experiment, mid-stream: 'Pause the video if you don't know the answer already. Pause the video and think about it. Have you paused?... Just talking to myself. That wasn't a pause — your own pause.'
Amit, just before quoting himself approvingly: 'Ajay, I have ranted and raved, which is my elite privilege. It is a luxury that I get to enjoy.'
Ajay producing an actual card: 'Because I'm a card-carrying economist — and here is my card.'
Amit on signalling: 'I often say those who signal the most virtue possess the least. And I have found this to be true especially of men. So watch out.'
Amit's drive-by aphorism on opinions: 'You've thought about that for 30 seconds. I have read about it for thirty years.'
'Luxury beliefs' — coined by Rob Henderson, the entire framing for the episode.
'Shoegaze' — the genre name, coined for bands whose guitarists stood still on stage staring down at their pedals to produce the sound.

'Hamara socialism achha tha' — Amit's mock-impression of an older Indian guest on his podcast bemoaning the loss of the socialist era. Played for the absurdity of nostalgia for a system that kept the country poor.
Boris and Igor — Pinker's two-Russian-farmers parable from Enlightenment Now: kill Boris's goat, end inequality. The cleanest illustration of the difference between equality and welfare.
Yes Minister — Amit invokes the show's classic line, paraphrased: 'We must do something. This is something. Let's do it.' His diagnosis of intellectually lazy elite policy.
'Bootleggers and Baptists' — Bruce Yandle's coinage for the unholy alliance between moralistic prohibitionists and the underworld that profits from prohibition.
Hansie Cronje — invoked as the era when match-fixing was at its worst, contrasted with the modern game where cricketers' legitimate earnings make the temptation lower.
Section 377 — the colonial-era anti-sodomy clause, struck down in 2018; remembered here as the legal hook that enabled the Matunga Racket.

Indira's preamble vs. Ambedkar's preamble — the framing for why young CAA protesters who wave 'the Constitution' are in fact waving Indira's words, not Ambedkar's, and unwittingly carrying 'socialist' along with 'secular.'
Chandra Bhan Prasad's two heroes — Ambedkar and Adam Smith. Used by Amit as the punchline showing that the late-1950s Ambedkar would have been at home with markets.
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' Communist Manifesto — Ajay's exercise: read the action checklist at the end of the book and notice how much of it is in modern India.
Nitin Pai's calculation — every 1% rise in Indian GDP per capita lifts roughly two million people out of poverty. The arithmetic that turns 'degrowth' into a concrete moral cost.
Walter Block's Defending the Undefendable — Amit's reading recommendation, chosen because Amit himself has just spent the episode defending sweatshops, prostitution, and gambling.
